findings.problem: The diff deletes the session_secret rotation that used to run on every successful password change in change_password(). Previously, `new_auth` updated both `password_hash` and `session_secret` with a freshly generated secret, which made `validate_session` reject every previously-issued cookie (triggarr/auth.py validate_session/sign_session are keyed on auth.session_secret), then re-signed and re-issued only the acting user's cookie under the new secret. Now `new_auth` only updates `password_hash`; `session_secret` is left untouched, so any cookie issued before the password change (including one held by an attacker who stole it, or a session on another device) continues to validate successfully after the password is changed. This is a targeted removal, not a refactor: the sibling token-based reset flow at routes.py (`/reset/confirm`, ~line 1937-1947) still performs the identical rotation with an explicit comment 'Rotate the session secret so every cookie signed with the old secret is invalidated immediately (D-12)', confirming the control is a deliberate, documented security requirement that this diff strips from the standard change_password path only, with no replacement. The removal is also directly contradicted by existing tests in tests/test_auth_routes.py: `test_change_password_rotates_session_secret_and_persists` (asserts the persisted secret changes and the old cookie fails validate_session), `test_change_password_reissues_acting_user_cookie` (asserts a fresh cookie is set), and `test_change_password_evicts_other_device_session` (asserts a second device's session is evicted) — all of which this change should break, which is independent confirmation this is a regression rather than an intentional behavior change.
findings.title: Password change no longer invalidates other active sessions (session-secret rotation removed)
findings.why_it_matters: Changing your password is the standard remediation when you suspect your session or credentials have been compromised (e.g. stolen cookie via XSS, a shared/lost device, or a leaked session token). With this control removed, an attacker holding a previously-issued triggarr_session cookie retains full authenticated access even after the legitimate user changes their password — defeating the entire point of the password-change feature as a compromise-recovery mechanism. There is no other control in this path that achieves the same effect.
